### Time-pressure rules

\* **Never drop an acceptance criterion merely to save time.**
\* Cut optional refactoring, abstractions, speculative cleanup, duplicate tests, commentary, and non-required documentation before cutting scope.
\* Do not perfect one criterion while untouched criteria remain.
\* If one blocker consumes roughly **20–30 minutes without material progress**, preserve evidence, continue independent in-scope criteria, then return to it.
\* At **60 minutes remaining**, stop optional refactoring and focus only on uncovered acceptance criteria, regressions, required documentation, AI attribution, and required validation.
\* At **30 minutes remaining**, make no discretionary changes. Finish unresolved in-scope work, required checks, AI records, and final scope verification.
\* If an external/repository blocker genuinely prevents full completion, do not pretend the issue is complete. Complete all independent in-scope work and report the exact blocked criterion and evidence.

### Scope ledger

Maintain a compact internal ledger equivalent to:

\| Acceptance criterion | Test first | Implementation | Validation | Docs/AI | Status |
\| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
\| AC1 | test/file | files | command | required/n-a | pending/in-progress/done |

Every acceptance criterion must reach \`done\` or have a concrete documented blocker before local review.

\---

\## 3. Git workflow

Follow \`docs/git-methodology.md\`.

Never develop directly on \`main\`.

Before a new issue:

\* update \`main\`;

\* create one branch for the issue.

Branch format:

\`\<type>/\<issue-number>-\<short-description>\`

Use only repository-approved branch types.

Normal commits must reference:

\`Refs #\<issue-number>\`

Codex may make \*\*as many local commits as useful without asking permission\*\*.

Keep commits:

\* issue-scoped;

\* logically focused;

\* accurately attributed;

\* consistent with repository methodology.

Do not rewrite existing history unless required and safe.

Never force-push \`main\`.

\---

\## 4. Push / PR permission gate

\*\*Never push or create a Pull Request without Dean's explicit approval.\*\*

Requests such as:

\* implement;

\* complete;

\* finish;

\* commit;

\* prepare;

\* get ready for review

do \*\*not\*\* grant push/PR permission.

When local work is ready, report:

\* implementation summary;

\* acceptance-criteria scope ledger showing every criterion as satisfied or concretely blocked;

\* commits;

\* changed files;

\* TDD evidence for behavioural changes: test added/changed, Red command/result, Green command/result;

\* tests/checks actually run;

\* documentation changes;

\* AI register status;

\* known limitations;

\* remaining Definition of Done work.

Then ask exactly:

\*\*May I push the branch and create the Pull Request?\*\*

Do not push or create the PR until Dean approves.

Approval to push/create a PR does \*\*not\*\* grant permission to merge or close the issue.

Every Pull Request must include an AI declaration that names only the AI tools and

models actually used for the work. This is required even when the repository's

AI register and commit trailers have also been updated.

\---

\## 5. Implementation rules

Before editing a file, it must contribute to:

\* an acceptance criterion; or

\* an applicable Definition of Done requirement.

Prefer the smallest correct change.

Inspect existing implementation and tests first and follow established patterns.

For behavioural changes, translate the relevant acceptance criterion into one or more automated tests **before** editing production code.

Use this implementation sequence:

1. identify the smallest observable behaviour required by the issue;
2. locate the correct existing test layer and test file;
3. add or modify a test for that behaviour;
4. run the narrowest test command and confirm the new test fails for the intended reason;
5. make the minimum production-code change required;
6. rerun the same test until it passes;
7. refactor only if useful and in scope, keeping tests green;
8. repeat for the next behaviour.

Do not batch several untested implementation changes before running the relevant tests.

For efficient completion:

\* prefer the smallest existing extension point that satisfies the acceptance criterion;
\* reuse existing fixtures, builders, factories, mocks, helpers, validators, schemas, error handling, and service/repository patterns;
\* avoid new abstractions unless required or they materially simplify multiple in-scope criteria;
\* combine closely related criteria in one implementation pass only when each retains explicit test coverage;
\* defer cosmetic refactoring until all acceptance criteria are implemented;
\* do not optimize performance unless required by the issue, an existing invariant, or a failing performance check;
\* avoid duplicate behavioural tests across layers unless each protects a distinct contract.

Do not:

\* opportunistically refactor;

\* reformat unrelated files;

\* rename unrelated code;

\* introduce unnecessary dependencies;

\* change schemas unnecessarily;

\* change public interfaces unnecessarily;

\* implement adjacent backlog features;

\* weaken tests.

Preserve backwards compatibility unless the issue requires otherwise.

Handle relevant validation and errors.

Do not invent requirements.

\---

\## 6. Architecture constraints

Respect repository architecture, approved ADRs, and COMS3011A requirements.

In particular:

\* frontend and backend remain separate;

\* application data goes through the team's handwritten HTTP API;

\* do not introduce generated application-data endpoints;

\* do not create another backend;

\* do not replace the established authentication architecture;

\* do not introduce conflicting technology unnecessarily.

If the issue conflicts with an approved architecture/security decision or compulsory course requirement, stop and report the conflict.

\---

\## 7. Testing and validation — TDD policy

Behaviour changes must be developed with **Red → Green → Refactor** TDD.

Use existing project frameworks, test layers, fixtures, mocks, and conventions.

Determine commands from repository configuration/documentation; do not invent commands.

For each behavioural change:

1. **Red**
   \* write or update the smallest relevant automated test first;
   \* run the narrowest applicable test command;
   \* confirm the test fails because the required behaviour is missing or incorrect;
   \* if the test passes immediately, determine whether the behaviour already exists or whether the test is insufficient before changing production code.

2. **Green**
   \* implement the smallest production change that satisfies the failing test;
   \* rerun the same narrow test;
   \* do not expand scope while making it pass.

3. **Refactor**
   \* refactor only when it improves the issue-scoped implementation;
   \* keep the tests green throughout;
   \* do not use refactoring as a reason to introduce unrelated cleanup.

For bug fixes:

\* first create a regression test that reproduces the reported defect;
\* confirm it fails on the pre-fix behaviour;
\* implement the fix;
\* confirm the regression test passes.

Choose the lowest useful test level first:

\* unit tests for isolated domain/service/repository/component behaviour;
\* API/integration tests for HTTP contracts, persistence boundaries, and module integration;
\* UI/component tests for rendered states and user interaction;
\* E2E tests for critical cross-system journeys where lower-level tests cannot provide sufficient confidence.

Do not replace a lower-level deterministic test with an E2E test when both would verify the same behaviour adequately.

During implementation:

\* run the narrowest relevant test after each Red or Green step;
\* prefer test-name, test-file, module, or workspace-scoped commands over full-repository suites;
\* keep existing affected tests green;
\* record the actual command and result needed to demonstrate the TDD cycle;
\* do not repeatedly run expensive full suites while acceptance criteria are still being implemented.

Use this **validation funnel** unless repository policy requires otherwise:

1\. new/changed test only;
2\. affected test file or module;
3\. affected workspace/package suite;
4\. repository-wide or CI-equivalent checks once the implementation is complete enough to justify them.

Before review:

\* run all applicable tests/checks reasonably affected by the change.

This may include:

\* targeted unit/integration/UI/E2E tests;
\* broader affected workspace test suites;
\* lint;
\* formatting;
\* type-check;
\* build;
\* static analysis;
\* \`git diff --check\`.

Never claim a Red or Green step occurred unless the corresponding command was actually executed and its result observed.

Never claim a check passed unless it was actually executed successfully.

Never disable, delete, skip, loosen, or weaken tests merely to obtain a passing result.

Never change assertions to match incorrect implementation behaviour.

If a required test/check cannot run, state why and do not fabricate TDD evidence.

\---

\## 8. Documentation

Update documentation only when the issue changes a documented:

\* behaviour;

\* API;

\* database schema;

\* security rule;

\* setup process;

\* dependency;

\* deployment process;

\* testing procedure;

\* architecture/interface.

Do not rewrite unrelated documentation.

Follow repository AI-writing rules and the COMS3011A AI policy where applicable.

\---

\## 9. AI attribution

Codex-generated or materially Codex-modified code must be attributed in the relevant commit.

Use:

\`\`\`text

\<type>(\<scope>): \<imperative description>

Refs #\<issue-number>

Assisted-by: Codex[ACTUAL MODEL USED]

\`\`\`

Use the \*\*exact active model\*\*.

Never guess the model or copy it from previous work.

If the exact model cannot be established, stop before committing affected code and ask Dean.

Only list AI tools/models actually involved in that commit.

\---

\## 10. Dean's AI register

Material Codex work retained in the repository must be recorded in Dean's AI register.

Default path:

\`evidence/ai/registers/dean-feldman.csv\`

If \`evidence/ai/registers/README.md\` defines another current Dean-specific path, use it.

Never modify another member's register.

Follow the register README exactly.

At minimum:

\* preserve the header;

\* quote every field;

\* use \`YYYY-MM-DD\`;

\* use semicolons inside fields instead of commas;

\* preserve valid CSV;

\* preserve trailing newline;

\* record only actual tools/models/work;

\* never invent transcripts, commits, PRs, tests, or verification.

Tool:

\`Codex\`

Model:

exact active model.

Verification/adaptation may contain only checks that actually occurred.

Do not claim Dean personally reviewed or verified work unless Dean explicitly confirms it.

Update the register as retained Codex work changes and include the update in an appropriate local commit.

Before requesting push/PR permission, verify the register accurately covers retained material Codex work.

\---

\## 11. Final local review

Before saying the implementation is ready:

1\. Re-read the issue and acceptance criteria.

2\. Reconcile the acceptance-criteria scope ledger. Every criterion must be implemented and evidenced or explicitly blocked with concrete evidence.

3\. Review changed files and commits.

4\. Confirm every behavioural acceptance criterion has appropriate automated test coverage.

5\. Confirm each behavioural change followed Red → Green → Refactor and that the observed Red/Green evidence is accurately reportable.

6\. Confirm every change is in scope.

7\. Check for accidental unrelated changes.

8\. Run applicable validation using the validation funnel and any repository-required final checks.

9\. Confirm required docs are current.

10\. Confirm architecture/course requirements remain satisfied.

11\. Confirm AI attribution is correct.

12\. Confirm Dean's AI register is current and valid.

13\. Inspect \`git status\`.

14\. Run \`git diff --check\` where applicable.

Report deliberately unimplemented follow-up work separately.

Keep the local-review report concise and evidence-based. Do not consume remaining execution time producing narrative that does not help verify scope, tests, commits, blockers, or Definition of Done.

\---

\## 12. Completion terminology

If implementation, TDD evidence, validation, local commits, documentation, and AI records are ready but the branch has not yet been pushed/reviewed, say:

\*\*Implementation ready for review\*\*

Do not describe the Gitea issue as complete until the repository's Definition of Done has actually been satisfied.

Typical remaining steps are:

\* Dean permission;

\* push & PR creation;

\* human/peer review;

\* CI;

\* merge;

\* issue closure.

Never fabricate evidence, tests, commits, reviews, PRs, stakeholder feedback, contributions, or AI records.

# Stat'sTheGame

Event-driven sports analytics platform providing validated submissions, derived statistics, dataset exports, and a versioned public API for COMS3011A.

[![Repository coverage](https://sdp.ms.wits.ac.za/git-push-pray/Sport-Analytics-Tool/raw/branch/coverage-badge/badge.svg)](https://sports-analytics-tool.pages.dev/testing/code-coverage/)

> **Current status:** The Express API validates Supabase identities, synchronizes provider-neutral application accounts, exposes the current user profile, and enforces `viewer`, `submitter`, and `admin` roles with competition-scoped submissions. Administrators can review users and manage submitter access. Approved submitters use the staged batch workflow for season and back-catalogue packages, with asynchronous validation, reference resolution, reviewer decisions, correction resubmission, and publication; administrators retain privileged direct/import routes. Public competition, season, fixture, event, competitor, participant, derived fixture-statistics, and participant season/competition/career aggregate reads are available without authentication. Filtered fixture-event and calculation-trace exports are available as JSON and CSV, and immutable versioned dataset releases can be generated and downloaded. External consumers can use administrator-issued API keys with per-minute rate limits and UTC daily quotas. The backend also provides the required runtime external API integration through Open-Meteo via `GET /api/v1/weather`. Advanced analyst-defined statistics, live-feed and bitemporal processing, change feeds, and other Advanced-tier functionality remain future work.

## Repository structure

```text
apps/frontend       React web application
apps/backend        Hand-written Node.js HTTP API
apps/worker         Independently deployable asynchronous ingestion worker
packages/contracts  Shared API schemas and TypeScript types
database            Migrations, seeds, and schema documentation
docs                Source for the public MkDocs documentation site
evidence            Stakeholder, sprint, testing, decision, and AI evidence
infra                Deployment and infrastructure documentation
scripts              Repository validation scripts
tests                Cross-application and non-unit testing assets
```

The frontend and backend are separate applications. The frontend may contact Supabase Auth for managed sign-in, but all application data must pass through the handwritten backend HTTP API. Generated Supabase data endpoints must not be used as the application API.

See [Repository Structure](docs/architecture/repository-structure.md) for the detailed tree and boundaries.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 20.19+ (20.x) or Node.js 22.12+; hosted CI/deployment use Node.js 22 LTS
- npm 10 or later
- Python 3.10 or later and MkDocs Material for the documentation site
- Access to the current Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL development database
- Access to the shared Supabase Auth project
- Docker Desktop or a compatible Docker Compose runtime only for the explicit container-based PostgreSQL integration-test workflow

> **Windows PowerShell:** Commands use portable `npm`/`npx` syntax. If PowerShell blocks
> `npm.ps1` or `npx.ps1`, use `npm.cmd` or `npx.cmd` instead, for example
> `npm.cmd run check`. Windows-specific file-copy commands are shown where needed.

## Getting started

This section is the complete quick-start path for a normal local checkout. For explanations,
troubleshooting and clean-clone verification detail, use the canonical
[Local Development Setup](docs/development/setup.md). If you are working on only one part of the
monorepo, use the [component guides](#component-guides) instead of repeating the whole setup.

### 1. Install dependencies

From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
```

### 2. Create local environment files

Real `.env` files are ignored by Git and must never be committed.

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
Copy-Item apps/backend/.env.example apps/backend/.env
Copy-Item apps/frontend/.env.example apps/frontend/.env
```

On macOS, Linux or Git Bash:

```bash
cp apps/backend/.env.example apps/backend/.env
cp apps/frontend/.env.example apps/frontend/.env
```

Populate the required values using the team's approved development configuration and the
[Environment Variables](docs/environment.md) guide. Do not place database passwords, elevated
Supabase keys or other server credentials in the frontend environment file.

### 3. Run the applications

Start the backend and frontend in separate terminals from the repository root:

```bash
npm run dev:backend
```

```bash
npm run dev:frontend
```

The asynchronous worker is started separately after its PostgreSQL, Service Bus, Blob and Azure
identity settings are configured:

```bash
npm run dev:worker
```

See [Azure asynchronous batch worker](docs/deployment/azure-worker.md) for the local dependency and
recovery walkthrough.

Once both are running, verify the local services:

- Frontend: [http://localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173)
- Backend health: [http://localhost:3000/api/v1/health](http://localhost:3000/api/v1/health)
- Current-user endpoint: [http://localhost:3000/api/v1/auth/me](http://localhost:3000/api/v1/auth/me)

The root development dispatcher also accepts the application name, so `npm run dev frontend` and
`npm run dev backend` are equivalent. Additional arguments are forwarded to the selected workspace
after `--`, for example `npm run dev frontend -- --host 0.0.0.0`.

### 4. Verify the repository

Run the normal database-independent quality gate:

```bash
npm run hygiene
npm run check
```

The separate hygiene command checks for unused monorepo files, dependencies and exports with Knip,
checks workspace dependency-version consistency with syncpack, and validates circular dependencies
and documented application boundaries with dependency-cruiser.

The normal database-independent test suite can also be run directly:

```bash
npm run test
```

To run every backend unit, API, and PostgreSQL integration test with the default disposable
PostgreSQL runtime, use:

```bash
npm run test:backend
```

Use `npm run test:backend:local` for the same backend workflow with the repository-managed Docker
Compose database instead.

PostgreSQL integration tests are explicit rather than hidden inside the normal gate. The standard

```bash
npm run test:database:local
```

Docker is not required for normal application development, `npm run test`, or `npm run check`.

execution modes.

## 1. Purpose

This document defines the Git methodology that will be followed throughout the development of the Sport Analytics Tool.

The methodology establishes:

- when commits must be created;
- how commit messages must be written;
- when branches must be created;
- how branches must be named;
- when branches may be merged;
- the requirements that must be met before merging;
- when project versions must be created; and
- how project versions must be named.

The purpose of the methodology is to maintain an organised repository, support effective collaboration, reduce merge conflicts, enable code review and provide traceability between requirements and their implementation.

All team members are required to apply this methodology consistently across all project repositories.

## 2. Selected Methodology

The team will use **GitHub Flow adapted for Gitea**.

Under this methodology:

1. `main` contains the latest reviewed and working version of the project.
2. Each significant unit of work begins as a Gitea issue.
3. A short-lived branch is created for the issue.
4. Development is completed through small, meaningful commits.
5. The branch, commits and Pull Request reference the issue.
6. A Pull Request is reviewed before it is merged.
7. Approved work is merged into `main`.
8. Important milestone states are identified using Git tags.

This methodology was selected because it provides sufficient control, traceability and peer review without introducing unnecessary permanent branches or administrative processes.

A more complex methodology, such as Git Flow, would require additional `develop`, `release` and `hotfix` branches. These branches are not necessary for the size, duration or release structure of this project.

The selected methodology is therefore intended to remain lightweight enough to be followed consistently by all team members.

## 3. The `main` Branch

The `main` branch represents the latest integrated, reviewed and working version of the project.

The following rules apply to `main`:

- Direct development on `main` is prohibited.
- Direct pushes to `main` are prohibited.
- Changes may only enter `main` through an approved Gitea Pull Request.
- `main` must remain in a buildable and working state.
- Force pushes to `main` are prohibited.
- Required automated checks must pass before a Pull Request may be merged.
- A Pull Request must be up to date with `main` before merge so the required status represents the
  integration state that will enter `main`.
- Milestone version tags may only be created from `main`.

The `main` branch will be protected using Giteaâ€™s branch-protection settings where these settings are available.
The protection should require `Sport Analytics CI / quality (pull_request)` and block merging an
out-of-date Pull Request. These protections are particularly important because post-merge CI performs
deployment-specific work instead of repeating the complete Pull Request application suite.

## 4. Gitea Issues and Traceability

Every significant development task must begin as a Gitea issue.

An issue must contain:

- a clear title;
- a description of the required work;
- acceptance criteria;
- an assigned team member;
- the relevant sprint milestone; and
- appropriate labels.

Examples of work that requires an issue include:

- implementing a feature;
- fixing a bug;
- creating or changing an API endpoint;
- changing the database schema;
- adding automated tests;
- configuring infrastructure or CI/CD;
- completing substantial documentation; and
- performing a technical investigation that will influence development.

Very small corrections, such as correcting a spelling error, may be included in an existing relevant issue.

Each significant change will follow the traceability chain below:

```text
Gitea issue â†’ branch â†’ commits â†’ Pull Request â†’ merge
```

For example, work related to issue `#12` would be recorded as follows:

```text
Issue:        #12 Validate event submissions
Branch:       feat/12-validate-event-submissions
Commit body:  Refs #12
Pull Request: #12 Validate event submissions
PR body:      Closes #12
```

This process allows the team to trace completed work back to its original requirement, implementation, review and final integration.

## 5. When to Create a Branch

A branch must be created when a team member begins work on a Gitea issue involving code, tests, configuration or substantial documentation.

Before creating a branch:

1. The related Gitea issue must exist.
2. The issue must have a clear description.
3. The issue must contain acceptance criteria.
4. The issue must have an assignee.
5. The issue must be assigned to the relevant sprint milestone.
6. The developer must update their local copy of `main`.

The branch must be created from the latest version of `main`.

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feat/12-validate-event-submissions
```

A branch should normally address one Gitea issue.

Where two issues cannot reasonably be separated, both issue numbers must be identified in the Pull Request description.

Branches must be short-lived. A normal branch should be completed within five working days. A branch may not remain open beyond the sprint in which it was created unless the delay and reason are recorded in the related issue.

If a branch becomes too large to review effectively, the work must be divided into smaller issues and branches.

## 6. How to Name Branches

Branch names must follow this format:

```text
<type>/<issue-number>-<short-description>
```

The approved branch types are:

| Type       | Purpose                                          |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `feat`     | New functionality                                |
| `fix`      | Correction of incorrect behaviour                |
| `docs`     | Documentation changes                            |
| `test`     | Test creation or modification                    |
| `refactor` | Code restructuring without a change in behaviour |
| `chore`    | Maintenance, setup or configuration              |
| `ci`       | Continuous integration or deployment changes     |

Examples include:

```text
feat/12-validate-event-submissions
fix/18-prevent-duplicate-statistics
docs/21-add-api-documentation
test/24-test-event-validation
refactor/31-extract-statistics-service
chore/7-configure-project
ci/9-add-backend-pipeline
```

Branch names must:

- use lowercase letters;
- contain the related issue number;
- separate words using hyphens;
- contain no spaces;
- use a concise but meaningful description; and
- reflect the main purpose of the branch.

## 7. When to Commit

A commit must be created whenever one small, logically complete unit of work has been completed.

Each commit must:

- represent one identifiable change;
- relate to the issue assigned to the branch;
- leave the affected section of the project in a working state;
- not knowingly introduce compilation or build failures;
- not knowingly cause existing tests to fail;
- exclude unrelated changes; and
- be understandable independently of later commits.

Examples of suitable commits include:

- creating the fixture database model;
- adding event-schema validation;
- implementing one API endpoint;
- correcting one calculation error;
- adding tests for one endpoint;
- updating the setup instructions for one service.

A commit must not combine unrelated work. For example, a single commit should not contain an unrelated API feature, user-interface redesign and documentation rewrite.

Developers must commit regularly and must not wait until an entire sprint or large feature has been completed before creating a commit.

Temporary commits may be used while work is in progress. However, commits with unclear messages such as `WIP`, `fix stuff` or `more changes` must not remain in a branch submitted for final review.
